laietani.t: The Iberian people of the coast around Barcelona, known later for the wines of Laietania and their coins minted at Barkeno.
laietani.o: The Laietani lived on the coastal plain and hills between the Llobregat and Tordera rivers, around modern Barcelona and the Maresme, from about the 5th century BCE. They formed part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and traded with Emporion and other Greek ports.
laietani.r: Their society was based on fortified hilltop towns such as Burriac and Puig Castellar, with grain storage silos and craft workshops. They minted coins with Iberian legends, including Laiesken and Barkeno. Under Rome their territory became famous for wine production, mentioned by Pliny and exported in amphorae across the western Mediterranean.
laietani.e: The Laietani were subdued during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and absorbed into Hispania Citerior. Their hill towns were gradually abandoned for Roman foundations on the plain such as Baetulo, Iluro and, under Augustus, Barcino, the origin of Barcelona.

lordship-of-mann.t: The Isle of Man under English lords, above all the Stanley earls of Derby, who ruled it as 'Kings' and then 'Lords of Mann' for over three centuries.
lordship-of-mann.o: After the Treaty of Perth of 1266 Man passed to Scotland, but it changed hands repeatedly in the Anglo-Scottish wars. From 1333 Edward III granted it to William Montagu, later Earl of Salisbury, and English rule became permanent. In 1405 Henry IV granted the island to Sir John Stanley.
lordship-of-mann.r: The Stanleys styled themselves Kings of Mann until 1504 and then Lords of Mann. The island kept the Tynwald, its own laws and the Manx language. James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby, held it for Charles I, and his wife, Charlotte de la Tremoille, defended it until 1651. Smuggling flourished in the 18th century because of low duties.
lordship-of-mann.e: The lordship passed to the Dukes of Atholl in 1736. To end smuggling, the British government bought the sovereign rights with the Revestment Act of 1765, creating the Crown Dependency of the Isle of Man.

lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.t: Frankish lordship of the Argolid, held by the lords of Athens and their heirs, which ended when its last lady sold it to Venice in 1388.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.o: After the death of Leo Sgouros, his last strongholds, Argos and Nauplia, fell to the Franks in 1212. The Principality of Achaea granted them to Otho de la Roche, lord of the Duchy of Athens, who held them as a fief of the prince.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.r: For a century the lordship was held by the dukes of Athens, giving them a foothold in the Peloponnese and a port at Nauplia. When the Catalans conquered Athens in 1311, Argos and Nauplia stayed loyal to the Brienne heirs of Walter of Brienne and later passed to the Enghien family. Greek and Albanian farmers worked the fertile Argive plain.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.e: Pressed by the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea and the Turks, the heiress Marie of Enghien sold the lordship to Venice in 1388. The Despot Theodore I seized Argos first, but Venice took control, creating Venetian Nauplia.

lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.t: Island lordship of the Venetian Ghisi family in the Cyclades, which ended when the last Ghisi bequeathed Tinos and Mykonos to Venice in 1390.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.o: The brothers Andrea and Geremia Ghisi, Venetian nobles, conquered Tinos and Mykonos around 1207 in the wave of private Venetian ventures that followed the Fourth Crusade. They also acquired other small islands, including parts of the Northern Sporades, and recognised the suzerainty of the Latin Empire and Venice.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.r: The Ghisi held the islands as a hereditary family domain, ruling from the hilltop castle of Exobourgo on Tinos over Greek farmers and fishermen, and were drawn into the feudal politics of the Triarchy of Negroponte and the Principality of Achaea. Byzantine raids under Licario in the 1270s cost them some islands.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.e: Turkish raids grew in the 14th century. Giorgio III Ghisi, the last of the line, died in 1390 and left his islands to Venice, which ruled Tinos until 1715 as Venetian Tinos.

latin-empire.t: Crusader state founded in Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204, a weak empire that lasted fifty-seven years.
latin-empire.o: The Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venetian interests and Byzantine politics, stormed Constantinople in April 1204 and plundered it. The crusaders elected Baldwin of Flanders emperor and divided the Byzantine lands: one quarter to the emperor, the rest split between Venice and the crusader barons, who received fiefs across Thrace, Macedonia and Greece.
latin-empire.r: The emperors ruled with Western feudal institutions, while Venice controlled a share of Constantinople and its trade. A Latin patriarch replaced the Orthodox one, alienating the Greek population. Baldwin I was captured by the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan at Adrianople in 1205. His brother Henry of Flanders proved an able ruler, but after him the empire shrank to little more than the capital.
latin-empire.e: Baldwin II pawned relics, including the Crown of Thorns sold to Louis IX, and even his son to raise money. In July 1261 troops of the Empire of Nicaea entered Constantinople, Baldwin fled, and the Byzantine Empire was restored.

lemovices.t: Gallic people of the Limousin who sent ten thousand men to relieve Alesia and whose name survives in Limoges.
lemovices.o: The Lemovices held the granite uplands of the western Massif Central, in the modern Limousin. Caesar lists them among the allies of Vercingetorix.
lemovices.r: Their land was rich in gold, which was mined in many small workings before the Roman conquest. Their main oppidum was at Villejoubert, near Saint-Denis-des-Murs.
lemovices.e: In 52 BCE they sent ten thousand men to Alesia, and their leader Sedullus was killed there. Under Rome their capital was Augustoritum, later Lemovices, from which come Limoges and the Limousin.

lyttos.t: Inland city of central Crete claiming Spartan descent, destroyed by Knossos in the Lyttian War of 220 BCE.
lyttos.o: Lyttos lay on a high plateau of central Crete, south-east of Knossos, and was one of the oldest cities on the island; it appears in Homer. Its people claimed to be colonists from Sparta, and ancient writers saw its customs as close to Spartan ones.
lyttos.r: Aristotle cites Lyttos as an example of the Cretan constitution with kosmoi, a council of elders and common messes. It controlled harbours on the north coast, including Chersonesos. Lyttos was a staunch enemy of Knossos and fought it repeatedly for leadership of central Crete.
lyttos.e: In the Lyttian War of 220 BCE Knossian forces destroyed Lyttos while its army was away. The city was rebuilt and resisted Rome until Metellus took it during the conquest of 69 to 67 BCE. It continued as a Roman town.

lato.t: Dorian hill city of eastern Crete with one of the best-preserved Greek town centres on the island, home of Alexander's admiral Nearchus.
lato.o: Lato stood in a saddle between two hills above the Gulf of Mirabello in eastern Crete. Founded by Dorian Greeks, it was a city by the 7th century BCE, named after the goddess Leto, whose image appears on its coins.
lato.r: Lato's remains include an agora, a prytaneion, a temple and stepped theatral area, showing the civic life of a Cretan polis with kosmoi magistrates. Nearchus, Alexander the Great's admiral, came from Lato. Inscriptions record its wars and treaties with neighbours such as Olous and Hierapytna.
lato.e: Lato's harbour, Lato pros Kamara, grew in importance in the Hellenistic period. After the Roman conquest of 67 BCE the hill town declined and the coastal settlement became the main centre, forerunner of modern Agios Nikolaos.

ligures.t: Ancient peoples of the north-western Mediterranean coast and Alps, from the Arno to the Rhône, who resisted Rome in their mountains for nearly two centuries.
ligures.o: The Ligures were among the oldest recorded peoples of north-western Italy and southern Gaul, already named by Greek writers of the 6th century BCE as living around Massalia and the Gulf of Genoa. Their origins are obscure; their language survives only in place names and personal names, and its relationship to Celtic and other Indo-European languages is debated.
ligures.r: They lived as separate tribes, among them the Ingauni, Intimilii, Apuani and Statielli, in hill forts and upland villages, combining herding, small-scale farming and raiding. Classical authors described them as hardy and poor. They served as mercenaries for Carthage, and along the coast they traded with Greek Massalia and the Etruscans, while inland groups mixed with Celtic neighbours.
ligures.e: Rome fought the Ligures from 238 BCE onward, deporting thousands of Apuani to Samnium in 180 BCE. The last Alpine groups were subdued under Augustus, whose Trophy at La Turbie (7–6 BCE) lists conquered tribes. The region became Augustus's Regio IX, Liguria, a name that survives in the modern Italian region.

lordship-of-sligo.t: The lordship of the O'Connor Sligo, a branch of the royal O'Connors of Connacht, who ruled northern Connacht from Sligo Castle.
lordship-of-sligo.o: The O'Connors of Connacht divided after 1384 into O'Connor Don, O'Connor Roe and O'Connor Sligo. The Sligo branch, descended from Brian Luighnech, controlled Lower Connacht, centred on the town and castle of Sligo.
lordship-of-sligo.r: O'Connor Sligo ruled over lesser lords such as the O'Haras, O'Dowds and MacDonaghs, frequently contesting the area with the O'Donnells of the Kingdom of Tir Chonaill, who often claimed overlordship of Sligo. The town held a Dominican friary and was a busy harbour.
lordship-of-sligo.e: Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585, Sir Donal O'Connor Sligo accepted English tenure. The family's power waned, and their estates were largely lost after the 17th century wars.

lusones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Tagus and Jalón, among the first to fight Rome in the Celtiberian wars of the early 2nd century BCE.
lusones.o: The Lusones lived on the high plateau around the sources of the Tagus and the Jalón, between modern Guadalajara and Zaragoza. Appian and Strabo count them among the Celtiberians, and they emerged in the later Iron Age.
lusones.r: Little is known of their society beyond their hillfort settlements and herding economy on the cold uplands. They appear in Roman narratives mainly as a source of fighting men in the wars of the 2nd century BCE.
lusones.e: In 181 BCE they took part in the First Celtiberian War, which ended with the treaty of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in 179 BCE. They were drawn into the later wars that ended with Numantia in 133 BCE and were then absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

lordship-of-ireland.t: The territory in Ireland held by English kings as lords of Ireland from Henry II's invasion of 1171 until Henry VIII took the title of king in 1542.
lordship-of-ireland.o: Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 to control Strongbow and other Norman adventurers. Irish kings and bishops submitted to him, and the papacy endorsed his claim. In 1177 he made his son John Lord of Ireland, a title merged with the English crown when John became king.
lordship-of-ireland.r: The lordship was governed from Dublin by a justiciar or lord deputy, with an Irish Parliament from the 13th century, English common law and shires. Norman lords built castles and towns, but from the 14th century Gaelic recovery and the Black Death shrank English rule to the Pale around Dublin, and the Statutes of Kilkenny of 1366 sought to stop settlers adopting Irish ways.
lordship-of-ireland.e: In 1541 the Irish Parliament declared Henry VIII King of Ireland, creating the Kingdom of Ireland in 1542.

latin-league.t: Alliance of the Latin towns around Rome, bound by shared cults and rights, that fought and then partnered Rome until Rome dissolved it in 338 BCE.
latin-league.o: The Latin peoples of the plain south of the Tiber shared a language, the cult of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount and other common sanctuaries from the early Iron Age. By the 6th century BCE they met in council at the grove of Ferentina and dedicated a federal shrine of Diana at Aricia, whose founding a Latin dictator, Egerius Baebius of Tusculum, is said to have led.
latin-league.r: The League was a loose association of towns such as Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Tibur and Praeneste, sometimes led by an elected dictator. Members shared rights of trade and intermarriage with each other. After Rome defeated the Latins at Lake Regillus around 496 BCE, the treaty of Spurius Cassius in 493 BCE made Rome and the League equal partners in defence, and they jointly founded colonies against the Aequi and Volsci.
latin-league.e: As Rome came to dominate the alliance, the Latins revolted in the Latin War of 340–338 BCE. Rome won, dissolved the League in 338 BCE and made separate treaties with each town. The shared 'Latin rights' survived as a legal status Rome later granted to colonies and provinces.

lampsacus.t: Phocaean colony on the Hellespont, famed for its wine and the cult of Priapus, where Epicurus taught and Anaxagoras died.
lampsacus.o: Lampsacus was founded by Phocaea c. 654 BCE on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, on a site said to have been offered by a local king. Its fertile hinterland produced wine that became the city's main export.
lampsacus.r: In the late 6th century BCE the tyrant Hippoclus and his son Aeantides ruled Lampsacus under Persia; Aeantides married a daughter of Hippias of Athens. Artaxerxes I granted the exiled Themistocles the city's revenues for wine. Lampsacus paid large tribute in the Delian League. Anaxagoras spent his last years there, and Epicurus taught in the city before moving to Athens.
lampsacus.e: Lampsacus appealed to Rome against Antiochus III in 196 BCE and became an ally. It passed into the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE. The modern town of Lapseki stands on the site.

latin-archbishopric-of-patras.t: Church-ruled state in the north-western Peloponnese, where the Latin archbishops of Patras governed the city as secular lords for over 150 years.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.o: The Latin archbishop of Patras was the senior Catholic churchman of the Principality of Achaea. Around 1276 the archbishops acquired the rights of the Barony of Patras, giving them lordship over the city and its land in addition to their spiritual role.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.r: The archbishops governed with the help of canons and knights, while acting as vassals of the princes of Achaea and increasingly as independent rulers under papal protection. Patras traded silk and currants with Italy. To defend themselves from the Turks and Byzantines, the archbishops placed the city under Venetian administration from 1408 to 1413.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.e: In 1429 Constantine Palaiologos, future last Byzantine emperor, took Patras from Archbishop Pandolfo Malatesta's officials, and the citadel surrendered in 1430. Patras joined the Despotate of the Morea until the Ottoman conquest of 1460.

lordship-of-chios.t: Genoese lordship of the Zaccaria family on Chios, granted by Byzantium to defend the island against Turkish raiders and lost to a Greek rising in 1329.
lordship-of-chios.o: Benedetto I Zaccaria, a Genoese admiral and merchant who already held the rich alum mines of Phocaea from the Byzantines, occupied Chios in 1304 to protect it from Turkish pirates. Emperor Andronikos II, unable to defend the island himself, recognised Zaccaria rule for a fixed term, which was later renewed.
lordship-of-chios.r: The Zaccaria ruled as nominal Byzantine vassals, but in practice as independent lords. They profited from the island's mastic, wine and silk and from alum trade. Martino Zaccaria built a fleet that fought Turkish raiders successfully, took the title King and Despot of Asia Minor from the Latin pretenders, and struck his own coins.
lordship-of-chios.e: Martino's growing independence alarmed the Byzantines. In 1329 the Chiots rose against him with the support of Andronikos III, who landed with a fleet; Martino was captured and Chios returned to Byzantium. The Genoese came back in 1346, creating the Maona of Chios.

lordship-of-galloway.t: A semi-independent Gaelic lordship in south-west Scotland, whose lords acted almost as kings until the line ended in 1234.
lordship-of-galloway.o: Galloway takes its name from the Gall-Gaidheil, the 'foreign Gaels' of mixed Norse and Gaelic descent who settled the region in the 9th and 10th centuries. Around 1110 Fergus of Galloway emerged as its ruler, styled king in some sources, and married an illegitimate daughter of Henry I of England.
lordship-of-galloway.r: The lords of Galloway ruled a land of cattle and sea-power with its own laws, while founding monasteries such as Dundrennan and Soulseat and reviving the bishopric of Whithorn. Fergus's grandson Roland and great-grandson Alan were great Anglo-Scottish nobles; Alan's fleet raided Ireland and the Kingdom of the Isles.
lordship-of-galloway.e: When Alan died in 1234 without a legitimate son, Alexander II divided Galloway between his daughters, crushing a revolt. The lordship became part of the Kingdom of Scotland; Alan's grandson was the future King John Balliol.

lordship-of-ameland.t: A Wadden Sea island that remained a free lordship under the Cammingha family, neutral in the wars around it, until the Orange-Nassau family bought it.
lordship-of-ameland.o: Ameland lay outside the authority of the counts of Holland and the Frisian lands, and from the 15th century the Cammingha family, Frisian chieftains, ruled it as lords, a status the register dates to 1424. They defended its independence against the Habsburgs and later the Dutch provinces.
lordship-of-ameland.r: The island was small, with villages such as Hollum, Ballum and Nes, living from fishing, farming and later whaling, with many 17th-century whaling commanders. Its lords claimed neutrality, which let islanders trade during wars. Ameland accepted the Reformation and governed itself through local courts under the lord.
lordship-of-ameland.e: After the Cammingha line ended, the lordship was bought in 1704 for the Orange-Nassau family. It lost its separate status in the Batavian period and became part of Friesland in the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

lordship-of-andros.t: Latin lordship on the Cycladic island of Andros, a vassal of the Duchy of the Archipelago that survived until the Ottoman takeover in 1566.
lordship-of-andros.o: Around 1207 the Venetian Marino Dandolo, a companion of Marco Sanudo, conquered Andros from the Byzantines and held it as a fief under Sanudo's Duchy of the Archipelago. The island was fertile and well placed on the sea route between Euboea and the central Cyclades.
lordship-of-andros.r: A small Italian elite held the castle and the best land, while Greek Orthodox islanders produced silk, wine and grain. The lordship passed among Venetian families, including the Ghisi, Sanudo and Zeno, and was disputed in dynastic quarrels with the dukes of Naxos. From 1384 the Sommaripa family, starting with Crusino I, ruled it for most of its remaining history.
lordship-of-andros.e: Increasing Turkish raids left Andros dependent on Venetian protection and Ottoman tolerance. In 1566, when the Ottomans removed the last Crispo duke of Naxos, they also ended Sommaripa rule on Andros, which was annexed to the empire.

lordship-of-beaujeu.t: The barony of the Beaujolais hills between Lyon and Mâcon, whose lords founded Villefranche-sur-Saône and served the French crown before it passed to the Bourbons.
lordship-of-beaujeu.o: The lords of Beaujeu appear in the 10th century as castellans in the hills west of the Saône, between the counts of Mâcon and Forez and the archbishops of Lyon. Their castle at Beaujeu gave its name to the Beaujolais, and they gradually brought the surrounding parishes under their control.
lordship-of-beaujeu.r: The lords built a compact barony and around 1140 founded Villefranche-sur-Saône, which became its commercial centre and later capital. Vineyards and the Saône trade underpinned its economy. Lords such as Humbert V, constable of France, rose high in royal service, and the family married into the houses of Forez and Savoy.
lordship-of-beaujeu.e: In 1400 the last lord, Edward II, childless and in debt, left the Beaujolais to Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, and it joined the Duchy of Bourbon. After the Bourbon lands were confiscated in 1527, it passed through several holders before ending up in the Orléans family.

lordship-of-utrecht.t: The former bishops' lands around Utrecht under Habsburg rule, where the Union of Utrecht, founding act of the Dutch Republic, was signed in 1579.
lordship-of-utrecht.o: Weakened by wars with Guelders and Holland, Bishop Henry of Bavaria transferred the temporal power of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht to Charles V in 1528. The Nedersticht became the Lordship of Utrecht, one of the Seventeen Provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-utrecht.r: Charles V built the Vredenburg castle in Utrecht to control the city and governed through a stadtholder shared with Holland. The province kept its own estates, with the cathedral chapters forming an influential first estate. The bishop remained a purely spiritual figure, and Utrecht became an archbishopric in 1559.
lordship-of-utrecht.e: Utrecht joined the Revolt; the citizens demolished Vredenburg in 1577, and the Union of Utrecht was concluded there in 1579. After the Act of Abjuration in 1581 it became a province of the Dutch Republic.

larissa.t: Chief city of Thessaly on the Peneios river, seat of the powerful Aleuad family and of the Thessalian League.
larissa.o: Larissa grew on a low hill by the Peneios in the plain of northern Thessaly, inhabited since the Neolithic. In the Archaic period it became the leading city of the Thessalian League under the Aleuad family, who claimed descent from Heracles. Aleuas the Red was credited with organising Thessaly into four districts.
larissa.r: Larissa's landed aristocracy ruled over serfs called penestai and bred horses for cavalry. The Aleuad Thorax supported Xerxes in 480 BCE. Later Larissa welcomed the sophist Gorgias, and Hippocrates died there. The Aleuads invited Philip II of the Kingdom of Macedon to intervene against the tyrants of Pherae.
larissa.e: From the 340s BCE Larissa was effectively under Macedonian control. After Flamininus proclaimed Greek freedom in 196 BCE it became the seat of the revived Thessalian League and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE; it is a major Greek city today.

lower-navarre.t: The fragment of the Kingdom of Navarre north of the Pyrenees, ruled by the Albret kings and the future Henry IV until its union with France in 1620.
lower-navarre.o: Ferdinand of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Navarre south of the Pyrenees in 1512. The Albret kings kept a small Basque-speaking territory on the northern side around Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port and Saint-Palais, which Charles V gave up around 1530 as too hard to hold.
lower-navarre.r: The Albret monarchs, who also ruled neighbouring Béarn, kept the royal title and Navarre's own estates and courts, with Saint-Palais as the seat of government. Queen Jeanne d'Albret converted to Calvinism and promoted it, though most Basques stayed Catholic. Her son Henry III of Navarre became Henry IV of France in 1589.
lower-navarre.e: Henry IV kept Navarre separate from France. In 1620 Louis XIII issued an edict uniting Lower Navarre and Béarn with the Kingdom of France, and French kings were styled 'King of France and Navarre' until 1830.

landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.t: Small Hessian landgraviate in the Taunus, home of the soldier-prince of Kleist's drama and later of a celebrated spa and casino.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.o: Hesse-Homburg was established in 1622 when Landgrave George II of Hesse-Darmstadt granted Homburg vor der Höhe to his brother Frederick I as an appanage. It remained dependent on Hesse-Darmstadt for most of its history rather than a fully sovereign state.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.r: Frederick II, who lost a leg in Swedish service and commanded the Brandenburg cavalry at Fehrbellin in 1675, built the baroque palace and inspired Heinrich von Kleist's play The Prince of Homburg. Later landgraves welcomed Huguenot and Waldensian refugees. In the 19th century Homburg grew into a fashionable spa, and its casino, opened in 1841, drew visitors from across Europe.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.e: Hesse-Homburg was mediatised to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1806 but restored as a sovereign member of the German Confederation in 1815, gaining Meisenheim. The line died out in 1866, the lands passed briefly to the Grand Duchy of Hesse and were then annexed by Prussia.

lordship-of-groningen.t: The city of Groningen and its surrounding Ommelanden under Habsburg rule, a reluctant province that joined the Dutch Republic only after a siege in 1594.
lordship-of-groningen.o: Groningen, a Hanseatic city that dominated the Frisian Ommelanden around it, resisted Saxon rule and placed itself under Charles of Egmond, duke of Guelders, in 1515. When Guelders weakened, the city and countryside accepted Charles V as lord in 1536, joining the Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-groningen.r: Stad en Lande, the city and the lands, was governed by its own estates in which the city and the rural Ommelanden constantly quarrelled over staple rights and taxes. The Habsburgs ruled through a stadtholder. Groningen traded grain and cattle and kept close ties with the German Hanse.
lordship-of-groningen.e: In 1580 the stadtholder Rennenberg went over to the Spanish side, keeping Groningen royalist. Maurice of Nassau besieged and took the city in 1594, and it joined the Dutch Republic as a province.

lordship-of-molina.t: A semi-independent Castilian lordship on the borders of Aragon, ruled by the Lara family and governed by its own celebrated fuero.
lordship-of-molina.o: Alfonso I of Aragon took Molina around 1129. It was soon granted to the Castilian noble Manrique Pérez de Lara, who held it under Castilian overlordship and in 1154 gave the town and its land a fuero, a charter of rights for settlers.
lordship-of-molina.r: Molina was a frontier lordship of herders and settlers between Castile and Aragon, defended by its great castle. Its lords issued laws, minted coins and raised troops with considerable autonomy. In the 13th century the heiress Mafalda married the infante Alfonso de Molina, brother of Ferdinand III, tying it closer to the Castilian royal family.
lordship-of-molina.e: Blanca Alfonso de Molina died childless in 1293, and the lordship passed to her half-sister María de Molina, queen of Sancho IV, and thus to the Crown of Castile. Spanish kings still bear the title Lord of Molina.

lordship-of-rhodes.t: Independent Byzantine lordship on Rhodes under the Gabalas family after the fall of Constantinople in 1204, later absorbed by the Empire of Nicaea.
lordship-of-rhodes.o: When the Fourth Crusade broke up the Byzantine Empire in 1204, the Greek official Leo Gabalas took control of Rhodes and neighbouring islands and ruled them as his own domain, styling himself Caesar and lord of Rhodes and the Cyclades.
lordship-of-rhodes.r: Gabalas ruled as an independent Greek lord with a fleet that let him trade and bargain. Under pressure from John III Vatatzes of Nicaea, who sent an expedition in 1233, he accepted Nicaean overlordship. In 1234 he made a treaty with Venice granting its merchants trading rights while securing Venetian support. His brother John Gabalas succeeded him around 1240.
lordship-of-rhodes.e: In 1248 the Genoese seized Rhodes in a surprise attack. Nicaea recaptured the island around 1250 and ruled it directly as part of the Empire of Nicaea. In 1310 it fell to the Knights Hospitaller, becoming Hospitaller Rhodes.

lebedos.t: Small Ionian city between Teos and Colophon, one of the twelve of the Ionian League, later home of the travelling Dionysiac actors.
lebedos.o: Lebedos was settled by Ionian Greeks, traditionally under Andraemon, son of Codrus, on the coast between Teos and Colophon c. 1000 BCE. Though small, it was one of the twelve members of the Ionian League.
lebedos.r: Little is known of its government. It lived from farming and fishing and had hot springs nearby. Lebedos fell to Lydia and then to the Achaemenid Empire, and paid tribute to Athens as a member of the Delian League. It revolted from Athens in 412 BCE.
lebedos.e: Lysimachus moved many of its inhabitants to Ephesus c. 290 BCE. The Ptolemies refounded it as Ptolemais, and the guild of Dionysiac artists later settled there. Lebedos passed into Roman Asia after 133 BCE; Horace described it as nearly deserted.

lugi.t: People of eastern Sutherland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name may honour the Celtic god Lugus.
lugi.o: The Lugi are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them in the far north of Scotland, usually located on the east coast of Sutherland around the Dornoch Firth and the Brora area, between the Decantae and the Cornavii (Caithness). Their name may derive from the god Lugus or from a word for raven.
lugi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. Eastern Sutherland has many brochs along its river valleys and coast, such as those of Strath Brora, suggesting communities led by local families who controlled grazing and farmland.
lugi.e: The Lugi vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts and then of the Norse earldom of Orkney before being drawn into the Scottish kingdom.

lordship-of-valencia.t: The Valencian principality of Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, who conquered the city in 1094 and held it against the Almoravids until his death.
lordship-of-valencia.o: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, a Castilian noble exiled by Alfonso VI, had built a mercenary career serving the Taifa of Zaragoza and collecting tribute in the east. When the qadi Ibn Jahhaf killed al-Qadir in 1092, Rodrigo besieged Valencia, which surrendered in June 1094.
lordship-of-valencia.r: El Cid ruled as an independent lord, nominally loyal to Alfonso VI. He defeated Almoravid relief armies at Cuarte in 1094 and Bairén in 1097, burnt Ibn Jahhaf alive and turned the great mosque into a cathedral under Bishop Jerome of Périgord. Most of the Muslim population remained, paying taxes to his garrison.
lordship-of-valencia.e: El Cid died in 1099. His widow Jimena held Valencia until 1102, when Alfonso VI judged it indefensible, evacuated the Christians and burnt the city. The Almoravids entered in May 1102. The story inspired the epic Cantar de mio Cid.

lordship-of-rimini.t: The Malatesta lordship of Rimini, home of Sigismondo Malatesta's Tempio Malatestiano and of the tragedy of Paolo and Francesca.
lordship-of-rimini.o: Malatesta da Verucchio, leader of the Guelphs of Rimini, drove out the Ghibelline Parcitadi family in 1295 and made himself lord of the city. His heirs ruled Rimini as papal vicars and spread through Romagna and the Marche.
lordship-of-rimini.r: The Malatesta were warlords and condottieri who governed Rimini, Cesena, Fano and other towns. Malatesta's son Gianciotto killed his wife Francesca da Polenta and his brother Paolo, a story Dante told in the Inferno. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, a brilliant and ruthless captain, had Leon Battista Alberti remodel the church of San Francesco as the Tempio Malatestiano. Pope Pius II publicly condemned Sigismondo in 1462 and took most of his lands.
lordship-of-rimini.e: In 1500 Cesare Borgia drove out Pandolfo IV Malatesta. Venice held Rimini from 1503 to 1509, after which it passed to direct papal rule in the Papal States.

lordship-of-clandeboye.t: A Gaelic lordship in Antrim and Down held by the Clann Aodha Buidhe O'Neills, who took over the lands of the collapsed Earldom of Ulster.
lordship-of-clandeboye.o: The Clann Aodha Buidhe, descendants of Aodh Buidhe O'Neill, a 13th century king of Tir Eoghain, moved east across the Bann after the collapse of the Earldom of Ulster in 1333. By around 1350 they ruled much of south Antrim and north Down, later divided into Upper and Lower Clandeboye.
lordship-of-clandeboye.r: The lordship's seat was the castle at Castlereagh near Belfast, and its chiefs ruled through Gaelic law, cattle wealth and Scottish gallowglasses. Their territory was later contested by the MacDonnells and by English colonisation attempts, including the Earl of Essex's massacre of Sir Brian MacPhelim O'Neill and his family in 1574.
lordship-of-clandeboye.e: Con O'Neill, the last lord, lost most of his lands to the Scots Hugh Montgomery and James Hamilton in 1605, opening north Down to large-scale Scottish settlement.

lordship-of-ainos.t: Branch lordship of the Genoese Gattilusi family at the mouth of the Maritsa, controlling trade from Thrace until Mehmed II took it in 1456.
lordship-of-ainos.o: Ainos (Enez), an old Greek port at the mouth of the Hebrus (Maritsa), came under the control of Niccolo Gattilusio, brother of Francesco I Gattilusio of the Lordship of Lesbos, around 1384. It became a separate branch of the family's possessions in the northern Aegean.
lordship-of-ainos.r: The lords of Ainos profited from salt pans, fisheries and river trade with the Thracian interior, and their realm included Samothrace and at times Imbros. They acted as Byzantine vassals and later as Ottoman tributaries. Palamede Gattilusio ruled for about forty years, and the family's inscriptions and fortifications survive on Samothrace and at Enez.
lordship-of-ainos.e: After the death of Palamede in 1455 a succession dispute among his heirs gave Mehmed II an excuse to intervene. In 1456 the Ottomans took Ainos and the lordship ended.

lusitania.t: The Roman province of western Iberia, roughly modern Portugal and Extremadura, governed from the splendid veteran colony of Emerita Augusta.
lusitania.o: Lusitania was carved out of Hispania Ulterior by Augustus after the Cantabrian Wars, with the division under way from 27 BCE. Its capital, Emerita Augusta (Mérida), was founded in 25 BCE for veterans of those wars. It covered the lands of the Lusitanians, Vettones and Celtici between the Douro and the Guadiana.
lusitania.r: An imperial legate governed the province, among them the future emperor Otho from 58 to 68 CE. Emerita grew into one of the great cities of the West, with its theatre, amphitheatre and long bridge over the Guadiana. Olisipo (Lisbon) and Pax Iulia (Beja) were other centres, and the economy rested on farming, mining and fish sauce. Christianity spread early; Eulalia of Mérida was martyred in 304.
lusitania.e: In 409 Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed into Hispania, and the Alans settled in Lusitania. In 439 the Suebic king Rechila took Emerita, ending effective Roman rule. The province's name later became a poetic name for Portugal.

lacetani.t: An Iberian people of inland Catalonia who resisted Rome during the Second Punic War and Cato's campaign of 195 BCE.
lacetani.o: The Lacetani lived in the interior of Catalonia, roughly in the modern comarques of Bages, Anoia and Solsonès, from about the 5th century BCE. They were part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and neighbours of the Ilergetes and Ausetani.
lacetani.r: Their society of fortified hilltop villages lived from farming and herding. Ancient writers, mainly Livy, record them only in wartime, and their name is easily confused with the coastal Laietani, so many details are uncertain.
lacetani.e: They fought the Romans under Gnaeus Scipio in 218 BCE and again in the north-eastern revolt of 197 to 195 BCE, when Cato stormed their chief town. Afterwards they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and their name faded.

lordship-of-brecknock.t: A marcher lordship in the Usk valley created by Bernard de Neufmarche's conquest of the Welsh kingdom of Brycheiniog.
lordship-of-brecknock.o: Bernard de Neufmarche invaded the kingdom of Brycheiniog in the late 11th century and killed Rhys ap Tewdwr of the Kingdom of Deheubarth near Brecon in 1093. He built Brecon Castle and founded Brecon Priory, granting lands to his followers.
lordship-of-brecknock.r: Brecknock was governed as a marcher lordship with its own courts and military obligations, a Norman lowland lordship over a largely Welsh upland population. It passed by marriage to the de Braose family and then to the de Bohuns, earls of Hereford, and later to the Staffords, dukes of Buckingham.
lordship-of-brecknock.e: Edward Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, was executed in 1521 and the lordship came to the crown. The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 made Brecknock a shire, which survives as part of Powys.

lordship-of-mechelen.t: A small separate lordship between Brabant and Antwerp that became the judicial and court capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-mechelen.o: Mechelen was long divided between the prince-bishops of Liège and the Berthout family, under constant pressure from Brabant. In 1333 the bishop sold his rights to Louis of Nevers, count of Flanders, and after disputes with Brabant the town became a distinct lordship, one of the seventeen provinces of the Low Countries.
lordship-of-mechelen.r: Mechelen was a prosperous cloth town with a tall cathedral tower of St Rumbold. Under the Burgundian State it became seat of the Parliament of Mechelen in 1473, later the Great Council, the supreme court of the Netherlands. Margaret of York and then Margaret of Austria, regent for Charles V, kept their courts there, making it a Renaissance centre.
lordship-of-mechelen.e: In 1559 Mechelen became the seat of the new archbishop, primate of the Netherlands. It stayed with the Spanish Netherlands and the Austrian Netherlands until French annexation in 1795, and is today a city of Belgium.

lilybaeum.t: Carthaginian fortress city at Sicily's western tip, founded after the fall of Motya, which withstood Pyrrhus and a nine-year Roman siege.
lilybaeum.o: After Dionysius I destroyed Motya in 397 BCE, Carthage settled the survivors on Cape Lilybaeum, the westernmost point of Sicily. The new city, on a headland with a sheltered harbour facing Africa, became Carthage's main base on the island.
lilybaeum.r: Lilybaeum was a heavily fortified port with walls, towers and a deep ditch. Its population was mainly Punic with Greek elements, and its trade linked Carthage with Sicily. It successfully resisted Pyrrhus in 276 BCE and, in the First Punic War, a Roman siege by land and sea from 250 to 241 BCE.
lilybaeum.e: Carthage ceded Lilybaeum to Rome by the treaty ending the First Punic War in 241 BCE. It became the seat of one of the quaestors of Roman Sicily, a post Cicero held in 75 BCE. It later became the Arab port of Marsa Allah, modern Marsala.

lucanians.t: Oscan-speaking people who took over much of southern Italy in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, conquering Greek Poseidonia and defeating Thurii.
lucanians.o: The Lucanians formed in the 5th century BCE from Samnite groups moving south into the mountains of modern Basilicata and the Cilento. They absorbed or displaced earlier peoples, the Oenotrians and Chones, and pressed the Greek cities of the coast, capturing Poseidonia around 410 BCE.
lucanians.r: They lived in fortified hill settlements such as Serra di Vaglio and Roccagloriosa, and were led in war by elected kings. Their federal sanctuary of the goddess Mefitis at Rossano di Vaglio has yielded Oscan inscriptions in Greek letters. Painted tombs at Paestum show armoured horsemen and funeral games. They defeated Thurii near Laus in 389 BCE and killed Alexander of Epirus at Pandosia in 331 BCE.
lucanians.e: The Bruttii broke away from them in 356 BCE. The Lucanians allied with Rome in 298 BCE, then turned against it with Pyrrhus and were subdued by 272 BCE. They later backed Hannibal and the Social War rebels, and their region became the Roman Lucania.

lordship-of-gower.t: A marcher lordship on the Gower peninsula and around Swansea, created by Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, in the early 12th century.
lordship-of-gower.o: Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, took Gower from its Welsh rulers around 1106 and built a castle at Swansea. English and Flemish settlers occupied the southern part of the peninsula, which developed a lasting English-speaking character.
lordship-of-gower.r: Gower was divided between an Anglicised lowland 'Englishry' and a Welsh upland 'Welshry'. The lords held their own courts and granted Swansea its first charter. The lordship passed to the de Braose family and later to the Mowbrays and the Herberts, and was repeatedly fought over by the lords of Glamorgan and Welsh princes.
lordship-of-gower.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 attached Gower to the new county of Glamorgan. Its distinct dialect and Anglo-Norman churches remain, and in 1956 it became Britain's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

lordship-of-ravenstein.t: A small lordship on the Maas that stayed outside the Dutch Republic and became a refuge for Catholics in a Protestant land.
lordship-of-ravenstein.o: Ravenstein grew around a castle on the Maas in north-eastern Brabant. In the 14th century it passed to the house of Cleves, and from 1360 it was held as a separate lordship by Cleves princes, independent of both Brabant and Guelders.
lordship-of-ravenstein.r: The Cleves lords of Ravenstein, notably Adolf of Cleves and his son Philip, were prominent at the Burgundian court. Later the lordship passed to the dukes of Jülich-Berg and the Palatinate-Neuburg family. When the surrounding lands came under the Dutch Republic, Ravenstein remained a Catholic enclave, where priests and believers from the Generality lands could worship freely.
lordship-of-ravenstein.e: The lordship was absorbed into the Batavian Republic around 1800, ending its separate status. It later became part of the province of North Brabant in the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

lordship-of-piedmont.t: The Savoy-Achaea principality in Piedmont, a cadet branch of the house of Savoy that also claimed the Frankish Principality of Achaea in Greece.
lordship-of-piedmont.o: In 1294 Count Amadeus V of the County of Savoy settled his nephew Philip with the family's lands in Piedmont as a dependent appanage. In 1301 Philip married Isabella of Villehardouin, heiress of the Principality of Achaea, and his line kept the title princes of Achaea even after losing Greece.
lordship-of-piedmont.r: Philip and his heirs ruled from Pinerolo over Turin and the towns of the upper Po plain, as vassals of the counts of Savoy. They fought the March of Montferrat and the Marquisate of Saluzzo for control of Piedmont and held assemblies of nobles and towns. Prince Louis founded the University of Turin in 1404.
lordship-of-piedmont.e: Louis died without a legitimate heir in 1418, and his lands returned to his cousin Amadeus VIII of the Duchy of Savoy, uniting Piedmont with Savoy. The heir to the Savoy throne was later styled Prince of Piedmont.

lordship-of-carpi.t: The Pio family's small Emilian lordship, whose humanist prince Alberto III Pio made Carpi a Renaissance showpiece.
lordship-of-carpi.o: In 1319 the Pio family, local nobles, took control of Carpi, a town between Modena and Mantua, with the support of the Bonacolsi. They ruled it as imperial vicars, with the Este and Gonzaga as powerful neighbours.
lordship-of-carpi.r: The Pio governed a small farming territory and its walled town. Alberto III Pio, pupil and patron of the printer Aldus Manutius, rebuilt Carpi around a huge new square with the castle, a new cathedral and porticoes. A diplomat at Rome, he sided with France in the Italian Wars and quarrelled with Erasmus. The family often divided the lordship among relatives.
lordship-of-carpi.e: Alberto's support for France cost him his state: Charles V's forces occupied Carpi, and in 1527 the emperor gave it to Alfonso I d'Este. Carpi then became part of the Este lands of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

league-of-corinth.t: Alliance of Greek states under Macedonian leadership created by Philip II after Chaeronea, the framework for Alexander the Great's invasion of Persia.
league-of-corinth.o: After defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II called the Greek states to Corinth in 338-337 BCE. They swore to a common peace, forbidding wars and revolutions among members, and named Philip hegemon of a war of revenge against Persia. Sparta alone refused to join.
league-of-corinth.r: A council (synedrion) of delegates, with votes roughly proportional to each member's military strength, met at Corinth and other festival sites and could judge disputes. Members kept their own governments, but Macedonian garrisons held Corinth, Thebes, Chalcis and Ambracia. Alexander had his leadership confirmed in 336 BCE and punished Thebes' revolt in 335 BCE in the league's name.
league-of-corinth.e: The alliance gave Alexander a Greek mandate for his Asian campaign. On news of his death in 323 BCE, Athens and the Aetolians led the Lamian War; Antipater's victory at Crannon in 322 BCE ended both the war and the league. Antigonus and Demetrius briefly revived it in 302 BCE.

lordship-of-the-isles.t: The MacDonald sea lordship of the Hebrides and western Highlands, a Gaelic power so strong its lords negotiated with England as near-independent princes.
lordship-of-the-isles.o: John of Islay, a descendant of Somerled of the Kingdom of Argyll and the Isles, styled himself Dominus Insularum, Lord of the Isles, from 1336. Through marriage and royal favour he united most of the Hebrides and much of the western mainland under Clan Donald.
lordship-of-the-isles.r: The lords held council at Finlaggan on Islay, with a council of the isles, and patronised the Iona abbey, galley-building, Gaelic poets and physicians. Donald of the Isles fought the Battle of Harlaw in 1411 over the earldom of Ross. John MacDonald II's secret Treaty of Westminster-Ardtornish with Edward IV in 1462 planned to partition Scotland.
lordship-of-the-isles.e: When the treaty was discovered, John lost Ross in 1475. In 1493 James IV forfeited the lordship, and the title was later annexed to the heir of the Scottish crown in the Kingdom of Scotland.

lordship-of-pesaro.t: An Adriatic lordship held by the Malatesta and then the Sforza, before passing to the della Rovere dukes of Urbino in 1512.
lordship-of-pesaro.o: A branch of the Malatesta of Rimini took control of Pesaro in 1285 and ruled it as lords and papal vicars. In 1445 Galeazzo Malatesta sold Pesaro to Alessandro Sforza, brother of Francesco Sforza, who had married his granddaughter Costanza da Varano.
lordship-of-pesaro.r: Under the Malatesta and then the Sforza, Pesaro was a small Adriatic court state living from farming, fishing and maiolica pottery. Alessandro Sforza and his son Costanzo built the Rocca Costanza fortress and patronised artists. Giovanni Sforza, Costanzo's son, married Lucrezia Borgia, but the marriage was annulled and Cesare Borgia expelled him in 1500. He returned after Pope Alexander VI's death in 1503.
lordship-of-pesaro.e: After Giovanni's son died young, Pope Julius II granted Pesaro in 1512 to his nephew Francesco Maria I della Rovere, joining it to the Duchy of Urbino.

leontini.t: Inland Chalcidian city of eastern Sicily on a rich grain plain, whose envoy Gorgias drew Athens into Sicilian affairs in 427 BCE.
leontini.o: Thucydides records that Chalcidians from Naxos, led by Theocles, founded Leontini in 729 BCE, expelling the native Sicels from the site. It lay on hills above the Leontine plain, one of the most fertile grain-growing areas in Sicily, a short distance inland from the sea.
leontini.r: Leontini's wealth came from grain. Around 610 BCE Panaetius became the first known tyrant in Sicily there. The city fell under Hippocrates of Gela around 495 BCE and later under Syracuse. Under pressure from Syracuse it sent the orator Gorgias to Athens in 427 BCE, and his speeches won an Athenian alliance and the first Athenian expedition to Sicily; Gorgias also helped bring Sicilian rhetoric to Greece.
leontini.e: In 422 BCE the Leontine aristocrats expelled the common people and moved to Syracuse, which absorbed the city. Its plight was a pretext for the great Athenian expedition of 415 BCE. Leontini was later revived as a dependent town and as Lentini survives today.

lusitanians.t: The fierce Iron Age people of central Portugal whose leader Viriathus defeated Roman armies for years before his murder in 139 BCE.
lusitanians.o: The Lusitanians lived between the Douro and the Tagus, in central Portugal and the neighbouring parts of Extremadura, emerging as a recognisable people in the second half of the first millennium BCE. They spoke Lusitanian, an Indo-European language known from a handful of inscriptions in Latin letters, such as those of Cabeço das Fráguas.
lusitanians.r: Lusitanian society was organised in clans and hillfort communities, with warrior bands under chosen leaders and a herding and farming economy in the uplands. Raiding into the richer south was a constant feature. They worshipped local gods such as Bandua and Endovelicus, and their warriors fought in light, mobile formations that troubled Roman legions.
lusitanians.e: After raids from 155 BCE, the Roman praetor Galba massacred thousands under a false truce in 150 BCE. Viriathus, a survivor, led resistance until he was assassinated in 139 BCE, after which resistance collapsed. Their land later became the Roman province of Lusitania, a name later revived as a poetic name for Portugal.

lordship-of-biscay.t: A Basque lordship ruled by the Haro family under Navarre and Castile, whose fueros and assembly at Guernica made it a byword for local liberties.
lordship-of-biscay.o: Around 1040 Íñigo López Ezquerra appears in records as the first count or lord of Biscay, a vassal of Navarre. His descendants, the López de Haro, held the lordship for more than three centuries, moving their allegiance between Navarre and Castile.
lordship-of-biscay.r: The lords ruled with the consent of the Juntas Generales, the general assembly that met under the oak of Guernica and guarded Biscay's fueros, or customary laws. The economy depended on iron mining, forges, shipbuilding and fishing. In 1300 Lord Diego López V de Haro founded Bilbao, which grew into its chief port.
lordship-of-biscay.e: In 1379 the lordship passed by inheritance to John I of the Crown of Castile, and from then on the kings of Castile ruled Biscay as lords. Its fueros survived until the 19th century.

locri-epizephyrii.t: Greek city in Calabria famed for the law code of Zaleucus, the earliest written Greek laws, and for its sanctuary of Persephone.
locri-epizephyrii.o: Locrians from central Greece founded Locri Epizephyrii, 'Locri of the West Wind', around 680 BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near Cape Zephyrion. Ancient writers said the settlers included slaves and women of noble families, a story that may reflect the status of women in the city's aristocracy.
locri-epizephyrii.r: Locri's laws, attributed to Zaleucus in the mid-7th century BCE, were reckoned the first written code in the Greek world and known for severe punishments. A council of a thousand governed the city. Its Persephone sanctuary yielded hundreds of painted terracotta plaques (pinakes). Locri defeated much larger Croton at the Sagras river and founded Hipponion and Medma. It was Syracuse's closest ally: Dionysius I married a Locrian woman, and Dionysius II ruled the city harshly from 356 to 346 BCE.
locri-epizephyrii.e: Locri became a Roman ally after the Pyrrhic War, went over to Hannibal and was retaken by Scipio in 205 BCE; the outrages of its commander Pleminius caused a scandal in Rome. It continued as a Roman town until abandoned in the early Middle Ages.

leuci.t: Gallic people of southern Lorraine around Toul, steady suppliers of grain to Caesar's armies.
leuci.o: The Leuci lived on the upper Moselle and Meuse, in the modern departments of Meurthe-et-Moselle and Vosges. Caesar mentions them among the peoples who supplied his army with grain in 58 BCE.
leuci.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land included sanctuaries that grew important under Rome, above all Grand, a great healing shrine of Apollo Grannus with a large mosaic and amphitheatre.
leuci.e: The Leuci seem to have stayed loyal during the revolts, and Rome gave them the status of a free civitas. Their chief town Tullum became Toul, later one of the Three Bishoprics.

lordship-of-verona.t: The Scaliger lordship that made Verona a power in north-eastern Italy, whose lord Cangrande della Scala sheltered Dante.
lordship-of-verona.o: After Ezzelino III da Romano died in 1259, the Commune of Verona chose Mastino I della Scala as its leader, and by 1262 he was effectively lord. His family, the della Scala or Scaligeri, made the office hereditary.
lordship-of-verona.r: The Scaligeri ruled Verona as lords and imperial vicars. Cangrande I, lord from 1311 to 1329, conquered Vicenza, Padua and Treviso and hosted the exiled Dante, who dedicated the Paradiso to him. Under Mastino II the lordship reached Lucca and Parma, but a coalition of Venice and Florence stripped most of it away in 1339. The family's Gothic tombs, the Arche Scaligere, and the Castelvecchio bridge survive.
lordship-of-verona.e: Family murders weakened the dynasty. In 1387 Gian Galeazzo Visconti seized Verona from Antonio della Scala and annexed it to the Lordship of Milan. Venice took the city in 1405.

lordship-of-overijssel.t: The eastern Hanseatic lands of the former bishopric of Utrecht, with Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, under Habsburg rule before joining the Dutch Republic.
lordship-of-overijssel.o: The Oversticht, the eastern part of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, was ruled by the bishops until 1528, when Bishop Henry of Bavaria handed his temporal power to Charles V. Overijssel then became one of the Seventeen Provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands, with Drenthe attached to it.
lordship-of-overijssel.r: The province was governed by estates of nobles and the three towns of Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, Hanseatic ports on the IJssel. Deventer was the birthplace of the Devotio Moderna movement and a centre of printing. The Habsburgs ruled through stadtholders but left the towns their privileges.
lordship-of-overijssel.e: Overijssel joined the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and, after the Act of Abjuration of 1581, the Dutch Republic, although Spanish troops held parts of it until the 1590s.

lordship-of-leo-sgouros.t: Short-lived domain of the Greek magnate Leo Sgouros in the north-eastern Peloponnese, the chief resistance to the Frankish conquest of southern Greece.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.o: Leo Sgouros inherited power as archon of Nauplia from his father around 1198, as Byzantine authority weakened. He seized Argos and Corinth, attacked Athens and Thebes, and married Eudokia, daughter of the deposed emperor Alexios III, gaining a measure of legitimacy as Constantinople fell to the Fourth Crusade in 1204.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.r: Sgouros ruled as an independent strongman from fortresses rather than through any formal state, using force and reputed cruelty, and dominating the Argolid, the Corinthia and the Isthmus. He tried to block Boniface of Montferrat at Thermopylae in 1204 but retreated to the near-impregnable citadel of Acrocorinth.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.e: Besieged by the Franks, Sgouros died around 1208, reportedly riding his horse off the cliffs of Acrocorinth. Its garrison held out until about 1210, and Argos and Nauplia until 1212, when they fell to the Principality of Achaea and became the Lordship of Argos and Nauplia.

lipara.t: Greek city on the Aeolian Islands, founded by Cnidians, whose citizens shared land in common and fought Etruscan pirates at sea.
lipara.o: Settlers from Cnidus and Rhodes, led by the family of Pentathlus, settled on Lipari, the largest of the Aeolian Islands north of Sicily, around 580 BCE after failing to found a colony in western Sicily. The island had been inhabited since the Neolithic, when its obsidian was traded widely.
lipara.r: According to Diodorus, the Liparaeans at first held land in common, some farming while others manned the fleet against Etruscan pirates, and their victories were celebrated with dedications at Delphi. The city prospered from its harbour, alum and sea trade, and its necropolis has yielded fine pottery and theatre masks.
lipara.e: Lipara came under Carthaginian control in the 4th century BCE and served as a Carthaginian naval base in the First Punic War. Rome captured it in 252 BCE. It remained a town of Roman Sicily, today Lipari.

lordship-of-lesbos.t: Genoese lordship of the Gattilusi family on Lesbos, a Byzantine-allied dynasty that ruled northern Aegean islands until the Ottoman conquest in 1462.
lordship-of-lesbos.o: The Genoese adventurer Francesco Gattilusio helped the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos regain his throne in 1354. In reward John gave him his sister Maria in marriage and the island of Lesbos as a dowry in 1355, making the Gattilusi hereditary lords of the island, with Mytilene as their capital.
lordship-of-lesbos.r: The Gattilusi acted as Byzantine vassals and relatives, adopting Greek ways and titles, while trading with Genoa. Their family extended its power to Ainos, Thasos, Lemnos and Samothrace. They profited from alum, grain and the Black Sea trade, and from the 1390s paid tribute to the Ottomans. Mytilene's castle was rebuilt in their time.
lordship-of-lesbos.e: After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Gattilusi remained as Ottoman tributaries. In 1462 Mehmed II besieged and took Mytilene; the last lord, Niccolo Gattilusio, was taken to Constantinople and later executed.

lordship-of-milan.t: The signoria through which the Visconti turned Milan into the strongest state in northern Italy, before buying a ducal title in 1395.
lordship-of-milan.o: In 1259 Martino della Torre was made lord of the people, turning the Commune of Milan into a lordship. The della Torre were challenged by Archbishop Ottone Visconti, who defeated them at Desio in 1277; his great-nephew Matteo I Visconti received the title of imperial vicar in 1294.
lordship-of-milan.r: The Visconti ruled through councils and appointed podestà while keeping communal forms. Azzone Visconti absorbed Bergamo, Cremona, Como, Lodi, Brescia and other cities in the 1330s. Archbishop Giovanni Visconti added Genoa and Bologna, and in 1359 Galeazzo II took Pavia. Gian Galeazzo Visconti overthrew his uncle Bernabò in 1385 and created a centralised state, beginning Milan Cathedral in 1386.
lordship-of-milan.e: In 1395 Gian Galeazzo bought the title of duke from Emperor Wenceslas, turning the lordship into the Duchy of Milan, which he expanded towards Tuscany and Umbria before his death in 1402.

lordship-of-imola-and-forli.t: A short-lived papal-nephew state in Romagna, famous for the defiant Caterina Sforza, who held out against Cesare Borgia.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.o: In 1473 Pope Sixtus IV acquired Imola for his nephew Girolamo Riario, who married Caterina Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza of the Duchy of Milan. In 1480 the pope added Forlì after the end of the Lordship of Forli.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.r: Girolamo ruled harshly and taxed heavily, and was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici in 1478. He was murdered in 1488 by the Orsi family; Caterina held the fortress of Ravaldino, saved the state and governed as regent for her son Ottaviano Riario, crushing her enemies. She dealt with Florence and Milan as an equal and became a celebrated figure.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.e: Cesare Borgia attacked in late 1499. Imola fell quickly, and in January 1500 Caterina was captured at Ravaldino after a fierce defence. Both towns became part of Cesare's Duchy of Romagna.

lordship-of-faenza.t: The Manfredi lordship of Faenza in Romagna, the town whose glazed pottery gave Europe the word 'faience'.
lordship-of-faenza.o: The Manfredi family led Faenza's Guelphs in the 13th century, and in 1313 Francesco Manfredi became lord of the city. The family ruled as papal vicars, though they lost and regained the city several times in the 14th century.
lordship-of-faenza.r: The Manfredi governed Faenza and neighbouring towns such as Imola for a time, often serving as condottieri for Florence, Milan or Venice. The town's maiolica workshops flourished in the 15th century, and their glazed earthenware gave French and English the name faience. Carlo II Manfredi rebuilt the cathedral and the town centre in Renaissance style.
lordship-of-faenza.e: In 1501 Cesare Borgia besieged Faenza, which surrendered; the young lord Astorre III Manfredi was taken to Rome and murdered in 1502. Venice held Faenza until 1509, when it passed to the Papal States.

lordship-of-meath.t: The great Anglo-Norman liberty of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy, centred on the castle of Trim.
lordship-of-meath.o: In 1172 Henry II granted the former Kingdom of Mide to Hugh de Lacy to balance Strongbow's power in Leinster. De Lacy built motte castles across the territory and began the great stone castle at Trim, which became the largest Norman castle in Ireland.
lordship-of-meath.r: Meath was a liberty with its own courts and officials. De Lacy settled English tenants, founded towns and abbeys and married a daughter of Ruaidri Ua Conchobair, the high king. He was killed at Durrow in 1186. His son Walter de Lacy recovered the lordship after a conflict with King John and held it until 1241.
lordship-of-meath.e: After Walter's death in 1241 the lordship was divided between his granddaughters, creating the liberties of Trim and Meath. Meath later formed the heart of the English Pale.

ligurian-republic.t: The French-sponsored republic that replaced the old Republic of Genoa in 1797 and was annexed to Napoleon's empire in 1805.
ligurian-republic.o: In May 1797 a democratic rising in Genoa, supported by France, overthrew the old aristocratic Republic of Genoa. By the Convention of Mombello in June 1797 Napoleon reorganised it as the Ligurian Republic, with a constitution on the French model.
ligurian-republic.r: The new republic abolished noble privilege, but the French controlled its policy and took its resources. In 1800 the Austrians and British besieged Genoa, held by General Masséna, causing terrible famine before the city surrendered shortly before Marengo restored French dominance. A new constitution of 1802 restored the title of doge, held by Girolamo Durazzo.
ligurian-republic.e: In June 1805 the Ligurian Republic was annexed to the French Empire. After Napoleon's fall the Republic of Genoa (1814) was briefly restored before Genoa passed to the Kingdom of Sardinia.

lombard-league.t: An alliance of northern Italian city-republics that defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176 and won self-government from the emperors.
lombard-league.o: In 1167, according to tradition in an oath sworn at Pontida, Milan, Cremona, Bergamo, Brescia, Mantua and other cities formed a league against Frederick Barbarossa, absorbing the Veronese League. Pope Alexander III supported it, and the new city of Alessandria was named after him.
lombard-league.r: The league was an alliance of communes with a council of rectors from member cities, a shared war chest and joint armies, rather than a single state. Its forces defeated Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176, forcing the Truce of Venice in 1177 and the Peace of Constance in 1183, which recognised the cities' rights to elect their own officials.
lombard-league.e: The league was revived in 1226 against Frederick II, who defeated it at Cortenuova in 1237 but failed to break the cities. After Frederick's death in 1250 it faded away, as the communes turned to wars among themselves and to rule by lords.

lordships-of-schonburg.t: Cluster of lordships in western Saxony held by the Schönburg family for six centuries, balanced uneasily between imperial immediacy and Saxon control.
lordships-of-schonburg.o: The Schönburgs were imperial ministerials from the Saale region near Naumburg. From about 1170 they were granted lands in the Pleissenland, the imperial territory around Altenburg, and built up lordships along the Zwickauer Mulde centred on Glauchau, later adding Waldenburg, Lichtenstein and Hartenstein. These were held directly from the Empire, which gave the family the standing of minor imperial lords.
lordships-of-schonburg.r: The lordships were ruled by several branches of the family from castles in Glauchau and Waldenburg, with small towns, farmland and later textile crafts in the valley. The family adopted Lutheranism in the 16th century. Their position was squeezed by the neighbouring Wettin rulers of Saxony, who held some Schönburg lands as fiefs and steadily claimed sovereignty over the rest.
lordships-of-schonburg.e: By the recesses agreed with the Electorate of Saxony, culminating in 1740, the Schönburgs accepted Saxon sovereignty while keeping special rights of administration and justice. These lingered into the 19th century, and the family remained major landowners in Saxony until 1945.

leucas.t: Corinthian colony on the Ionian island of Lefkada, which cut a canal through its isthmus and later became the capital of the Acarnanian League.
leucas.o: Corinthians led by a son of the tyrant Cypselus founded Leucas c. 640 BCE on what was then a peninsula of Acarnania. The colonists dug a canal through the isthmus, making it an island. Its white cliffs at Cape Leucatas were linked with the legend of Sappho's leap.
leucas.r: Leucas stayed close to Corinth, fighting at Salamis in 480 BCE and with Corinth at Sybota in 433 BCE, and was a member of the Peloponnesian League. It was an oligarchy living from trade along the route to Italy. In the Hellenistic period it joined the Acarnanian League and became its meeting place.
leucas.e: After the Third Macedonian War Rome separated Leucas from Acarnania in 167 BCE, and it came under Roman control. The island is today's Lefkada.
leucas.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Leucatas

lordship-of-cortona.t: The Casali family's lordship over the Tuscan hill town of Cortona, which ended when the king of Naples sold it to Florence.
lordship-of-cortona.o: Cortona, an Etruscan hill town above the Valdichiana, had long been a self-governing commune and gained its own bishop in 1325. That year Ranieri Casali, head of a leading local family, became lord of the city, which the Casali then ruled as a hereditary lordship.
lordship-of-cortona.r: The Casali governed a small territory of hill and plain between Arezzo, Siena and Perugia, balancing between these neighbours and seeking imperial and papal recognition. Family murders over the succession were common. Little is known of their administration beyond the town's walls and the fortress they built.
lordship-of-cortona.e: In 1409 King Ladislaus of Naples captured Cortona from the last Casali lord during his wars in central Italy. In 1411 he sold the town to the Republic of Florence.
